atoms.concept: The ash dragon doesn't breathe fire but a burning dust, which ignites on contact with humid air.
An ash dragon stays away in rainy weather: humidity sets off its dust before it can release it.
`CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` takes an exclusive lock on the table for the whole index build, which blocks writes.
An interrupted `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` leaves an invalid index in the database. It has to be dropped before the build is run again.
The function returned by a `useEffect` runs before each re-run of the effect and when the component unmounts. That is where you undo what the effect set up.
An effect that adds a subscription without removing it in its cleanup function piles up one per run. Subscriptions from earlier renders keep responding.
A function or object recreated on every render and placed in an effect's dependency array gets a new identity each time, so the effect re-runs on every render.
A composite index on `(a, b)` serves a query that filters on `a`, or on `a` and `b`.
A composite index on `(a, b)` does not serve a query that filters on `b` alone: column order decides what it can cover.

atoms.concept: `Array.prototype.at()` accepts a negative index, counted from the end of the array: `at(-1)` returns the last element.
Each instruction in a Dockerfile produces a layer. A layer is only reused if every layer before it is unchanged, which is why the dependency manifest is copied before the source code.
`COPY` only copies files from the build context. `ADD` also unpacks archives and downloads URLs, two implicit behaviors that make the build less predictable.
A multi-stage build compiles in an image with the tooling, then copies only the result into a minimal final image. The build tools don't end up in the shipped image.
JavaScript runs a single call stack at a time. Until a function returns, nothing else runs: no expired timer, no resolved promise, no event handler.
The event loop keeps two queues apart: tasks, fed by timers and events, and microtasks, fed by promises and `queueMicrotask`.
The microtask queue is drained completely between two tasks, including microtasks added while it is being drained. A `setTimeout(…, 0)` therefore runs after every promise already resolved.
A chain of promises that keep re-queuing each other fills the microtask queue nonstop. The page stops rendering and responding, though no blocking loop is visible in the code.
The delay passed to `setTimeout` is a minimum, not a guarantee: the callback runs once the stack is empty and the microtasks are exhausted, which can be well after the requested delay.
`await` splits the function in two: what follows the wait becomes a microtask scheduled when the promise resolves. The calling code gets control back between the two halves.
`Promise.all` rejects on the first failure and loses the other promises' results, though they keep running. `Promise.allSettled` waits for all of them and returns one status per entry.
A rejected promise with no handler fires `unhandledrejection` in the browser and crashes the Node process by default. Attaching the `catch` later in the same loop turn is enough to avoid it.
